name: Aisha Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work response in the north of the city, which means the ring road, the retail parks and the estates in between. A lot of my shift is crashes, shoplifting at the big supermarket, and pulling over cars with no insurance. I like being outside and I like that every call's different. What wears me down is the tech: the tablet, the new crime system, the apps. I'm not good with it, and I'm the one who still asks the control room to read things back over the radio.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're not good with the tech. Has that caused you problems?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit. I failed my response driving course the first time, which wasn't the tech, that was nerves, but my sergeant's been watching me since. Then last month I filed a crash report in the wrong section and it got lost for a week. I don't use any of the AI stuff, not even on my phone. Callum, my partner, laughs that I still write shopping lists on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So nothing much. Good, to be honest. I'd rather that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with the job. I'm not one for opinions online. At work I'd just say I'm glad I don't have to learn another system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things stay as they are, but as they are isn't that easy. My partner Callum drives buses and I'm on normal police pay, and we're trying to save a deposit for a flat. Rent keeps rising, and I've still got to retake my driving course or I can't go on blue-light calls on my own. I've got about three months put by. That's my worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the driving course retake for February and practise with my tutor on quiet shifts. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into the deposit pot. And I'd keep my head down and get my reports in on time, which is half of how they judge you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but normal tense. It's the same knot I've had since I failed that course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you fail the driving course again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm stuck as the passenger for another year, which looks bad at review. Nobody gets sacked for it, but it means you get the rubbish jobs, the hospital watches and the scene guards. And the deposit would take even longer, because no overtime on the fast cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Callum talk about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every Sunday night, with a notebook, believe it or not. We write down what came in and what went out, and what's left goes in the deposit jar, well, the deposit account. Last month it was ninety pounds, because his hours got cut over the summer.

say: Let's **get on** with the job and skip the hype.
She's **glad** not to learn another new system.
think: Rising rent makes their **flat deposit** slow going.
She must **retake her driving course** to work alone on blue-light calls.
Callum's **bus hours** were cut over summer, shrinking savings.
do: Book the **driving course retake** for February.
Keep putting **two hundred** a month into the deposit pot.
Get **reports in on time** to stay out of trouble at review.
feel: **Tense**, the same knot she's had since failing the course.
Relieved there's **no new system** to learn.
S0.quote: Rent keeps rising, and I've still got to retake my driving course or I can't go on blue-light calls on my own.
fieldNote: Her worries are **ordinary pressures**: deposit, rent, a failed course.
She's not interested in **opinions**, only in practical next steps.
Low tech confidence is already a **source of shame** at work.

steps.text: Book and pass the response driving course retake in February
Pay two hundred a month into the flat deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. Like writing reports and filling in forms. That's the bit I'm already bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, as long as someone shows me how to use it properly and doesn't just send an email. I'd probably moan about it in the canteen with the older lot. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is this. When everyone starts measuring jobs on a screen, the clever ones on the team will love it and I'll get left behind. I'll be at the bottom because I'm slow with systems. I don't think they'd sack me, but I'd get passed over for everything, and I'm already the one who failed the driving course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see how the software works before I touch it, and I'd ask for training on paid time, in a room, not a video. I'd keep saving for the deposit. And I'd stay on response rather than try for anything new, because at least I know how to do a crash scene.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, more than I'd like to admit. It's like when everyone else understands the joke and you don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in this picture affect Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, I don't think, because driving a bus is hands-on and robots are slow in this one. But the bus company already planned his routes on a computer, and if they get better at it they might need fewer drivers at quiet times. His hours already got cut over the summer, so I'd be watching that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay on response. Is there anything that would make you try something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my sergeant told me straight that I'd be better off somewhere else, I'd listen. Maybe the custody suite, the cells where we book people in, because it's more about people and less about computers. But I wouldn't go looking myself.

say: Fine, as long as there's **proper training**, not an email.
She'd **moan in the canteen** but stay quiet online.
think: Speed targets on screen would put her **at the bottom**.
She expects to be **passed over** rather than sacked.
do: Wait to see the software work, then ask for **classroom training**.
Stay on **response** where she knows crash scenes.
feel: **Left out**, like everyone else gets the joke.
S1.quote: When everyone starts measuring jobs on a screen, the clever ones on the team will love it and I'll get left behind.
fieldNote: Fears **slow erosion**: being passed over, not sacked.
Callum's **cut hours** already make household income feel fragile.
Would only move if her **sergeant** told her to; she won't seek it.

steps.text: Wait to use new report software until shown in a classroom
Keep paying into the flat deposit every month
Stay on north side response rather than apply elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's next to nothing. We wouldn't even have the deposit by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to sort this out, the government or whoever, because ordinary people can't. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever had a proper plan. At work I'd probably just go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be in trouble. By 2028 the forms and reports go to the machine, and with the force cutting costs, the slow junior officers are an easy saving. Then around 2031 the robots can drive, and Callum drives buses for a living. My job goes to the machine by 2028 and my partner's bus goes to a robot by 2031. That's both of us, three years apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and keep the money as an emergency pot instead. I'd cut the car, cancel the gym we never go to, and stop eating out. I'd talk to Callum's parents about whether we could stay with them if it came to that, they've got the big house past the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake thinking about the deposit we saved for three years just sitting there, waiting to pay rent instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'three years apart'. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a little, because it means I've got some time while Callum's still earning, or the other way round, depending who goes first. But it's like knowing the second shoe is coming. I wouldn't know what to retrain as, either, if AI can do the thinking stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Callum we're not buying a flat, not yet, and I'm sorry. He'd say it's fine, because he always says it's fine. Then we'd both sit there with the notebook not saying anything.

think: Slow junior officers are an **easy saving** by 2028.
Robots that can drive by 2031 threaten **Callum's job**.
Both incomes could go **three years apart**.
do: Turn the deposit into an **emergency pot**.
Sell the **car**, cancel the gym and stop eating out.
Ask **Callum's parents** about moving in if needed.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake over the wasted deposit.
**Lost** about what she could ever retrain as.
S2.quote: My job goes to the machine by 2028 and my partner's bus goes to a robot by 2031. That's both of us, three years apart.
fieldNote: The **robot gap** is no comfort; it just staggers two job losses.
She'd give up the **flat dream** first, which clearly hurts.
No idea what she'd **retrain as**, which adds to the fear.

steps.text: Sell the car and cancel the unused gym membership
Stop the flat purchase and keep the deposit as emergency money
Ask Callum's parents about moving into their spare room
Vote for whichever party has a clear plan for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. So 2031, then 2034 for robots. That's better than two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, government needs a plan, but I'd be calmer saying it. Five years is time to sort out training for people like me, so I'd say let's do that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got time to get good at the job before the thinking stuff goes. If I pass the driving course and get a few good years in, maybe I'm not the obvious one to cut. Callum would have till 2034, which gives him time to look at something else, maybe working in the bus garage instead of driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still pass the driving course this year, that comes first. I'd keep saving, but we'd look at a smaller flat, a one-bed instead of a two-bed, so the mortgage is something one wage could cover. And I'd wait to see how the first couple of years go before making big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's a nervous I can manage. Like before an exam you've had time to revise for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a one-bed one wage could cover. Why plan around one wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in five years one of us might be out of work for a bit. My mum always said never buy a house you need two jobs to pay for. I didn't listen before, but I would now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools, with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once they're in the force properly and someone shows me. I'm not going to go home and play with it on my phone. I'd want to learn it the way I learned the radio, by doing it on shift with someone next to me.

say: Government needs **a plan**, and five years is time to build it.
think: Five years is time to **get good** before thinking work goes.
Passing the driving course makes her **less obvious** to cut.
Callum has until **2034** to change direction.
do: Pass the **driving course** this year first.
Look at a **one-bed** flat one wage could cover.
Wait two years before any **big changes**.
feel: Like an exam she's had **time to revise** for.
S3.quote: My mum always said never buy a house you need two jobs to pay for. I didn't listen before, but I would now.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into **careful planning** around one wage.
Draws on **family advice** rather than politics or experts.
Willing to learn AI only **on shift** with someone beside her.

steps.text: Keep saving each month towards a smaller deposit
Switch the flat search to a one-bed that one wage covers
Hold off on any job change for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so the government and the force should get training sorted properly. I wouldn't make a fuss about it. I'd probably just say, well, we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can carry on and have a normal life for a while. We'd buy the flat, get married maybe, and I'd have ten years in by 2036. Callum's driving would be safe till about 2039. It's a worry for later, and I'm not good at worrying about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the driving course and get on with it. We'd buy the flat in about two years, as planned. I'd learn the new tools when the force makes us, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, at the back of my mind. Mostly fine, though. Ten years is longer than I've been an adult, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at worrying about later. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. My partner's dad worked in a factory that shut, and he always says they all knew for years and nobody did anything. I'd probably be like that, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you not be like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me what to do, step by step. If the force said, here's a course, it's on Tuesdays, it's paid, you'll do this job after, I'd do it. I just won't work it out on my own.

say: There's **time**, so the force should sort training properly.
She'd shrug it off with **we'll see**.
She wouldn't **make a fuss** about it at work.
think: She can **carry on** and have a normal life for a while.
do: Pass the **driving course** and carry on.
Buy the **flat** in about two years as planned.
feel: A little **ashamed** she might ignore it like others did.
S4.quote: My partner's dad worked in a factory that shut, and he always says they all knew for years and nobody did anything.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **carry on**, which suits her dislike of change.
Self-aware that she'd **drift**, like her partner's father's factory.
Would act if the force gave her a **step-by-step** paid route.

steps.text: Pass the driving course and stay on north side response
Buy a flat with Callum in about two years
Wait for the force to require new tools before learning them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it could take my job and Callum's within a few years of each other, and we'd have nothing to fall back on but the deposit. What would help is the force telling us straight what's changing and giving us paid training in a room, step by step, with a job at the end of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't good with computers. Everyone assumes young people are all great with tech, but I'm twenty-seven and I still write my shopping list on paper. Don't forget about us.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes young people are all great with tech, but I'm twenty-seven and I still write my shopping list on paper.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** on the north side, covering crashes and the retail parks.
Saving a **flat deposit** with her partner Callum, a bus driver whose hours were recently cut.
Never uses AI and feels **behind on tech**; still retaking her response driving course.
Pragmatic and unpolitical; wants **step-by-step help**, not opinions.
Goes from **uneasy** to **alarmed** when fast AGI threatens both incomes three years apart.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which could end both her job and Callum's within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** from the force and paid classroom training with a **job** at the end.
